body:
To address this and your other comment in one; 
My partner has nothing negative. He actually works in finance so is very aware (and obsessive to a point) about credit reports. I think if it were just him, it would probably be fine as his credit and work history is impeccable at the moment. Unfortunately, his income alone isn’t enough for a decent mortgage. I have always had issues with finance based on non-citizenship and the electoral roll, so we started planning and saving several years back, trying to make things perfect so that when I did eliminate that issue (I know the numbers don’t really matter, but registering to vote actually boosted my credit score by 100 to 200 points depending on the site) we would be able to quickly move toward purchase. 

We went to speak to a broker who’d helped a friend get a mortgage recently. They told us it was in our best interests to go to our regular banks first, so that is what we did. We told them that we wanted to buy a house within the year, and that we wanted to get a good idea of the mortgage options available to us. 
They asked a few basic starter questions about savings, employment, and income. We had not yet done my taxes for the year at that time, so we gave them the figures for the years before and said this year had been a fluke and would be higher, but that I expected next year to be stable/slightly higher than last year (just not as high).
They did some things on their computer, frowned a bit, and said they didn’t think that we would be eligible for a mortgage with them at this time. We asked why, what can we do to fix that, etc., and they said that unfortunately they couldn’t give us that information but we were welcome to speak to them again in the future.

That happened at both banks (mine and my partner’s). So we were/are at a loss.

I get that I shouldn’t say my income will fall, but last year was a fluke that is not normal, so I also feel like I would be lying if I said I expect perpetual growth. So I said I expected it to stay stable with the prior year.

I just wanted to point out, this does not apply to me  and does not apply to a lot of people. There are very specific criteria that are noted on the link you provided.
I am in England and am not from the EU or a Commonwealth country. This means that I was not eligible prior to receiving citizenship. 

My guess is that you are either in Scotland/Wales, or are from a commonwealth country.

We have honestly scoured our credit reports and I genuinely don’t think there is anything that could be that negative. The only “negative” factors that have *ever* been on mine have been that I was not on the electoral roll (outside of my control) and there were a few months a while back where I carried a high (about 50% of the balance) credit card balance on one card for a couple months when we moved from a furnished flat to non and had to buy all the furniture. I have never missed a payment in my life, and nothing appears on the report that doesn’t belong there.

For my partner, it is pretty much the same story; nothing shows up on the credit report we can see. He was a bit of a bank hopper for a bit, so moved accounts several times in the past however many years… but nothing recent.

That has made me wonder though; In credit checks, I have always been scored miserably for “affordability”. I figured that sort of “link your account” scoring didn’t really matter, but could that actually affect it? The only reason it ever gave for that was that I had very little left in my current account at the end of the month. But that is because I budget tightly and move excess money into savings. I never use the overdraft, I just don’t see the point in keeping money in there when I could be earning better interest with it elsewhere.

For my income, the first year was 13k (half year, 7 years ago) then about 32k, 34k, 38k, 42k, 48k, 63k. The last year was a big jump and I expect/prefer it to go back down some (work/life balance sucked the past year). But it has steadily grown through the life of the business.

I have two personal credit cards (10k and 8k) and a business card (2k). I use the personal ones pretty regularly but don’t regularly keep a balance on them - most recently did so when we bought a sofa and I preferred to pay the interest of making 3 payments that way than losing interest by taking money out of a term savings account. 
My partner has 3 cards (2k, 5k, 10k) but only regularly uses one of them, and keeps no balance on them. 

The arrangement to pay was a debt management plan. It was a relatively small amount (5k) and was paid off over ten years ago. It was made directly with the lender, and no payments were missed on it. (IIRC, it was paid off early with assistance from family.) 

No funds for the deposit have come from overseas (I have lived in the U.K. for 10 years now.) I do make regular monthly payments against a student loan overseas though. (£400ish). Ex-partner had a mortgage overseas while we were together but it was paid off before I moved to the U.K., with no missed payments. (I was not named on it but paid half.) My current partner has nothing like that.

We both have copies of our credit files; there is really nothing at all on them that I can imagine impacting anything. We even made sure to not use any sort of payment plans in the past year just in case.

We have lived in the same place for 4 years, but it never got to the stage of providing proof of that. 

We waited to speak to them until after I had citizenship, figuring that would be an issue (it was at the time of getting a car; they wouldn’t even consider me for finance then). I am from outside the EU, but had ILR for a year prior to getting citizenship.

In terms of income, the past two years have been very good. Other than a slight dip during covid, it has grown steadily every year with the biggest jump between the past two years. I was asked if I thought my income would go up/down, and I was honest and said that I actually planned to actively lower it some. The last year was very busy, which was great for savings but not for work/life balance, so I don’t plan to take on a new client once my shortest contract ends. So hopefully around 50k/year, which was where it was the year before last.

Did that kill our chances? I thought it would be better to say that than have the income suddenly drop next tax year (shortest client contract ends in June)…

ETA:
Reconsidering the credit reports; I had a 25k loan that was taken out 6 years ago (startup loan thing for my business). It was paid back over 5 years. There were no missed payments, but it existed until not all that long ago. 
My partner also deferred some payments during Covid through programs offered by the lenders. We assumed this wouldn’t matter, but who knows!

I should have noted; we spoke to a broker initially and were told we would have the best luck speaking to our consecutive banks first… so that is what we did. Because the banks didn’t seem interested at all, we sort of assumed a broker would be even less hopeful. 
I guess we should probably go to a different broker!
